registry_rule: A PARAMETER-level comparison: what each model ASSUMES about benefit take-up, not what either model outputs. It stages NO value claims. The rates originate with DWP and HMRC (#86/#91) — UKMOD's table is a transcription of those plus mid-point choices of its own, and is recorded here as comparison context with its originator named, never as a scoreable claim.

engine_pin.pin_meaning: The pin follows the certified populace-uk bundle (==2.89.2), which is the engine these parameters are read from and the engine the scorecard computes in.
engine_pin.pin_rule: Read from importlib.metadata at write time, never typed as a literal.

gov.dwp.housing_benefit.takeup.engine_description: Share of eligible Housing Benefit recipients that participate. By definition, this is 100%, because only current claimants are eligible (no new claims).
gov.dwp.housing_benefit.takeup.why_one: NOT an assumption of full take-up. The engine's own description says the eligible population is restricted to existing claimants — 'By definition, this is 100%, because only current claimants are eligible (no new claims)' — so participation among them is 100% BY CONSTRUCTION. This is a closed legacy benefit, and the value is a cohort artifact of the denominator, not a modelling choice about behaviour.

ukmod_assumptions.source: UKMOD Country Report 2023-2030, CeMPA WP 8/26, Table 3.4 (assumed take-up probabilities)
originating_sources: DWP (2020) Income-related benefits: estimates of take-up
HMRC (2019) Child and Working Tax Credits take-up rates 2017-18
Scottish Fiscal Commission (December 2024) for devolved payments
ukmod_assumptions.transcription_note: SECOND-HAND. These are UKMOD's stated assumptions, which are themselves drawn from the DWP/HMRC/SFC publications named above, taking the mid-point where a range is published. Recorded as context for the comparison, never as a claim to score against — the first-hand figures belong to their originators.
ukmod_assumptions.mechanism_note: UKMOD applies take-up at HOUSEHOLD level per benefit, allocating first to units observed receiving in the data and then randomly (extension BTO, on by default). PolicyEngine's are national scalars. The mechanisms differ, so the comparable object is the ASSUMED AGGREGATE RATE, not the algorithm.
ukmod_assumptions.staleness_note: UKMOD flags its own rates as decaying: DWP and HMRC have not updated working-age take-up statistics since 2021, and CeMPA writes 'we have, as yet, failed to identify a suitable remedy'.
ukmod_assumptions.comparability_note: UKMOD models these as OPEN programmes on a 2023/24 FRS base, so its Housing Benefit, Income Support and tax-credit rates are not comparable with PolicyEngine's closed-cohort 1.0 values. Only the Pension Credit rows are a like-for-like comparison on the UKMOD side.

not_a_conclusion: This registry does NOT claim PolicyEngine's outputs are wrong, and after the #131 review it does not claim its take-up assumptions are deficient either. Four of the seven parameters are structural, not assumptions. For the three that are assumptions, a difference in an input is not an error in an output: policyengine-uk-data applies reported-recipient anchoring and fits weights to receipt-based DWP/OBR targets, either of which may move the result. Establishing output error needs #76.
the_finding:
NARROWED after review. v1 of this registry reported that PolicyEngine 'assumes full take-up' for Housing Benefit, Income Support, Child Tax Credit and Working Tax Credit, and compared those 1.0 values with UKMOD's non-take-up rates of 0.32-0.96. That was WRONG, and unfair to PolicyEngine. All four are CLOSED legacy benefits: the engine restricts eligibility to existing claimants, so 1.0 is definitional, not an assumption. Comparing it to an open-programme rate is not like for like. Caught by DTrim99 on PR #131; the rationale was in the parameters' own descriptions, which v1 read the values of without reading.

What survives is narrower and genuine. Three parameters are real assumed rates on programmes that are open, and carry no closed-cohort note: Universal Credit 0.55, Pension Credit 0.70, income-based JSA 0.56. Universal Credit is the substantive one — 0.55 against the 0.80 the Resolution Foundation states for the shared Landman/PERU model and the 0.82 recorded for that model in the Scottish Government's appendix. That is a 25-27 point spread on the largest working-age benefit, between open-programme rates that ARE comparable.
comparability_rule: A closed-cohort parameter may NOT be compared with an open-programme take-up rate. The denominators differ: one is participation among existing claimants, the other take-up among everyone entitled. The validator refuses a comparison that crosses that line.
divergence_axis: take_up_denominator: a closed-cohort parameter counts participation among EXISTING CLAIMANTS, while an open-programme rate counts take-up among everyone ENTITLED. Any comparison that crosses those denominators measures the difference in population, not in behaviour, and must be refused rather than named (#59).
